fast.topic: The Monday fast hour covers the whole of GST_112 Week 1 in a single pass, since the available material is only the MIVA recap deck. It opens with culture defined as a complex system of traditional behaviours, beliefs, practices and values, and drills the three fundamental components - technological (material culture), sociological (institutions and norms), and ideological (beliefs and values) - which is the week's most examinable list. It then moves to society, categorised into communal and associational forms, distinguished on three fixed bases: division of labour, social interactions, and traditions. Next it takes the historical emergence of society through two lenses: Karl Marx's vision of a communist society built on collective ownership of the means of production and distribution of wealth, and functionalism's view of society as an organism in which each component plays a crucial role. It then covers the impact of colonialism on African societies - specifically its alteration of governance, culture and family structures, using pre-colonial Yoruba communities as the worked example. The hour closes on nation-building, defined as mobilising resources for socio-economic and political development while constructing a national identity, and on national integration: why it matters for a diverse country, Nigeria's ethnic-diversity hurdle, and government initiatives to foster unity. Reference facts are drilled at the end: Cosmas Odinaka's 2020 study on nation-building and national integration, and the University of Lagos Centre for General Studies text Nigerian Peoples and Cultures (Lagos, 2013).

deep.topic: This session takes Week 1 conceptually. It covers what problem-solving in computer science is and why a computer demands a systematic approach - the computer contributes volume, speed and efficiency, not method, so the programmer must first know how a human solves the problem. It establishes what makes a problem a computational problem: a step-by-step solution with well-defined inputs, limitations and output conditions. It treats the four steps to problem-solving as four distinct jobs rather than a list to recite, and works through what each of algorithm, pseudocode and flowchart actually is and what each buys you - including why pseudocode that cannot be compiled or executed is still worth writing. It examines the three required properties of an algorithm's steps (ordered, unambiguous, complete) and what specifically breaks when each is absent, and it looks at decomposition, why it works and where it stops working. It then covers the translator chain of interpreter, compiler and assembler, the difference between debugging and testing, and the three error types of syntax, logical and run time. It closes on the two kinds of program documentation, why documentation begins at problem analysis rather than after the program works, and on refactoring - what it must preserve, what it changes, and when a change is not a refactor at all. fast.topic: The Wednesday fast hour covers GST_122 Week 1, "Language Skills", which establishes listening, speaking, reading and writing as the four building blocks of effective communication. It fixes the course's exact definition of each skill: listening is understanding, interpreting and responding to spoken language; speaking is articulating thoughts, ideas and information coherently and effectively; reading is comprehending, interpreting and analysing written text; and writing is conveying thoughts, information and emotions through written language. It draws the distinction between hearing and listening, and between active listening (full engagement, as in a lecture) and passive listening (merely hearing without deep comprehension, as with background music). On speaking, it covers the components of oral communication - clear pronunciation, appropriate tone, audience engagement, voice control, body language and delivery - worked through a persuasive-speech structure and two contrasting job-interview answers. On reading, it covers reading comprehension as grasping main ideas, context and subtext, using the passage "The Dangers of Faking Mental Health Issues" and its four takeaways. On writing, it names the four writing styles: persuasive, descriptive, narrative and expository. The hour closes with the marketing-team case study on emotive language and precision, and the claim that combining the skills strengthens critical thinking, engagement with complex discourse and a global perspective. Focus effort on stating definitions verbatim and on classifying given examples to the right skill or style, since that is how the course examines.

fast.topic: The Thursday fast hour covers PHY_108 Week 1, the review of the equation of a straight line and error analysis that underpins every practical report this semester. It starts with y = mx + c - identifying the dependent and independent variable, reading the gradient from two points on a best-fit line, the y-intercept c, and the x-intercept as -c/m. It then drills linearisation: converting T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) into T^2 against L with slope 4*pi^2/g, N = N0*e^(-lambda*t) into ln N against t with slope -lambda and intercept ln N0, y = kx^n into log y against log x with slope n and intercept log k, plus the Hooke's law, Coulomb's law and Boyle's law rows of the same table. Next it covers the graphing rules that carry marks in a lab report - sensible scaling, labelled axes with units, accurate plotting, and a single best-fit line rather than dot-to-dot. The error half defines error as the difference between measured and true value, separates systematic from random error with their sources, and gives absolute error, relative or fractional error, percentage error and the signed percentage difference. It closes with the Week 1 case study idea that the mean of repeated measurements is the most likely value, and the Ohm's law framing from the week summary where V is plotted against I so the gradient gives the resistance. Work one numerical example end to end: gradient to g to percentage error.

deep.topic: This session takes the same week-1 material and works it as problems. It covers converting between a net charge and a number of transferred electrons using q = ne; tracking charge through transfers, including the averaging rule q' = (q1+q2)/2 for identical conducting spheres in contact and following a charge through two successive contacts; and computing Coulomb forces with attention to squaring the separation and converting centimetres to metres. It covers adding forces and fields as vectors, including the case of two equal and opposite charges whose contributions at the midpoint reinforce rather than cancel, and finding the point on a line where the resultant field vanishes. It covers computing the field of a point charge and the force it exerts on a charge placed in it, including the direction reversal for a negative charge. It also covers diagnosing a wrong route from the shape of a formula, and checking a result by units and by order of magnitude. Constants used throughout: k = 8.99x10^9 N.m^2.C^-2, e = 1.6x10^-19 C.

Includes the two slide errors — the table on slide 22 and the word 'exponentially' on slide 21.

questions.q: The deck's SUMMARY slide defines a function. Which phrase carries the whole definition?
options: A relation that assigns exactly one output value to each input value
A relation that assigns at least one output value to each input value
A relation that assigns exactly one input value to each output value
Any set of ordered pairs of real numbers
questions.concept: The two clauses in the definition of a function
questions.why: Both halves do work: 'each' means no input is left unassigned, and 'exactly one' means no input is sent to two different places. Option 2 drops the uniqueness clause, which is precisely the condition that separates a function from a general relation. Option 3 reverses input and output — outputs are allowed to repeat, and slide 5 shows nothing wrong with several inputs sharing an output. Option 4 is the definition of a relation, the outer circle on slide 9, with no condition at all.

questions.q: Slide 9 draws 'functions' as a circle sitting inside a larger circle labelled 'relations'. What does that nesting assert?
options: Relations are the special case: every relation is a function
Functions are relations with an extra condition, so every function is a relation but not every relation is a function
Functions and relations are two names for the same collection
Neither contains the other; they merely overlap
questions.concept: Why containment runs one way only, function to relation
questions.why: A relation is any set of ordered pairs; a function is a relation that additionally sends each input to only one output. Imposing an extra condition can only shrink a collection, so functions land inside relations. Option 1 reverses it — the pair set with (1, 2) and (1, 4) is a relation that fails the condition. Option 3 ignores the drawing, which would then be one circle. Option 4 would require a function that is not a relation, and there is none, because every function is by definition made of ordered pairs.

questions.q: On slide 5, f(x) = x² is drawn from the domain {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. The values 17, 23 and 19 also appear in the picture but no arrow reaches them. What are they?
options: Part of the domain that f happens not to use
Part of the range, since they appear in the diagram
Part of the codomain but not the range — offered as possible outputs, never actually produced
A misprint; nothing unreached should be drawn
questions.concept: Range is what is hit, codomain is what is offered
questions.why: The codomain is the target set declared in advance; the range is the subset the rule genuinely produces, here {1, 4, 9, 16, 25}. Option 1 puts them on the wrong side of the arrows — the domain is the left-hand set of inputs. Option 2 is the standard confusion the slide exists to prevent: appearing in the picture is not the same as being an output. Option 4 misreads a deliberate teaching device as an error; the leftovers are the whole point of drawing a codomain at all.

questions.q: Slide 8 asks 'IS THIS A REAL-VALUED FUNCTION?' over a diagram whose output set is {K, 3, 9, 8, 6}. What makes this a real-valued question rather than merely a function question?
options: The domain has only four elements, which is too few for a real-valued function
Some outputs are never reached, so the mapping fails to be onto
The inputs are letters, and a function must always take numbers as inputs
One of the outputs is the letter K, and real-valued means every output must be a real number
questions.concept: What the word 'real-valued' adds to 'function'
questions.why: 'Function' constrains the arrows, one out of each input; 'real-valued' constrains the destination, the outputs must be real numbers. K is not a number, so whatever the arrows do, the mapping is not real-valued. Option 1 invents a size requirement the deck never states. Option 2 describes being onto, which the deck does not teach and which is irrelevant to the word 'real-valued'. Option 3 looks at the wrong end: it is the values, meaning the outputs, that must be real.

questions.q: In Domain Example 2 she writes x² + 5 ≠ 0, then x² ≠ −5, then concludes D = (−∞, ∞). What licenses that conclusion?
options: No real number squares to a negative, so x² = −5 has no real solution and nothing has to be excluded
−5 lies outside the domain, so it is removed and everything else survives
The numerator 3x + 1 is defined everywhere, and the numerator is what fixes the domain
x² + 5 is always larger than 3x + 1, so the fraction never becomes undefined
questions.concept: Why an impossible exclusion leaves the domain whole
questions.why: Her own NOTE says the square of a positive or a negative number is always positive. So the equation that would have created an exclusion has no real root, and the exclusion list is empty. Option 2 confuses a value of x² with a value of x — the −5 was never a candidate input. Option 3 states the rule backwards: the numerator places no restriction at all, only the denominator does. Option 4 compares the wrong things; a fraction is undefined when the denominator is zero, not when it is smaller than the numerator.

questions.q: In Range Example 3 she goes from |x − 3| ≥ 0 to −|x − 3| ≤ 0. Why does the inequality turn round?
options: Because an absolute value becomes negative once a minus sign is attached to it
Because both sides were multiplied by −1, and multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses its direction
Because zero is its own negative, so the direction of the sign is arbitrary at that line
Because the next step adds 2, and adding to both sides requires reversing first
questions.concept: Which operations reverse an inequality and which do not
questions.why: Multiplication by a negative reverses; addition of a constant does not. That is why her next line, adding 2 to both sides, keeps the sign as ≤ and delivers y ≤ 2. Option 1 mislabels the fact — the absolute value is still non-negative, it is the negated expression that is non-positive. Option 3 draws a false general rule from the fact that this particular right-hand side happens to be 0. Option 4 inverts the truth: adding never reverses, and this is exactly the distinction that separates R = (−∞, 2] from the wrong answer [2, ∞).

questions.q: Her inverse recipe reads: let y = f(x), switch x with y, then isolate the y variable. What does the switching step actually accomplish?
options: It renames the letters so the algebra looks tidier, and carries no mathematical content
It reflects the graph of f in the x-axis
It swaps the roles of input and output, so isolating y afterwards expresses the original input in terms of the original output
It converts f into 1/f, since swapping is another way of writing a reciprocal
questions.concept: What 'switch x with y' means, not just what to write down
questions.why: An inverse answers the reversed question — given the output, what was the input? Swapping the letters installs the old output in the input slot, so the rearranged equation is the reversed rule, ready to be read as a function of x. Option 1 is how the step is usually memorised and why it is misapplied to solve for the wrong letter. Option 2 names the wrong reflection; inversion reflects in y = x, not in the x-axis. Option 4 confuses the inverse with the reciprocal — for f(x) = 3x − 7 the inverse is (x + 7)/3 while the reciprocal is 1/(3x − 7), which are different functions.

questions.q: Why does the deck compute both f ∘ g and g ∘ f for the same f(x) = 5x − 4 and g(x) = x², side by side on one slide?
options: To show that the two agree once both are fully expanded
To show that composition is only defined when the functions are taken in one particular order
Because computing g ∘ f is a shortcut on the way to computing f ∘ g
To show the answers differ — 5x² − 4 against 25x² − 40x + 16 — so composition depends on the order
questions.concept: Composition is not commutative, demonstrated by one example pair
questions.why: Same two functions, two orders, two different polynomials — one quadratic with no linear term, one with −40x. That single comparison is the whole lesson of the slide. Option 1 is the belief the slide is written to destroy; test it at x = 1, where the values are 1 and 1, and at x = 2, where they are 16 and 36. Option 2 is false: both orders are perfectly well defined here. Option 3 invents a dependency; the two are computed independently, each by dropping one rule into the other's x-slot.

questions.q: Slide 5 draws three sets around f(x) = x². Name all three, say which elements belong to each, and explain in one sentence how the range and the codomain differ.
questions.concept: Domain, codomain and range as three separate sets
questions.why: A good answer names the domain as the set of inputs, {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; the range as the set of outputs the rule actually produces, {1, 4, 9, 16, 25}, which is the set she labels on the slide; and the codomain as the declared target set, containing those five outputs together with 17, 23 and 19, which no arrow reaches. The distinction to state: the codomain is announced in advance and may be generous, while the range is computed from the rule and consists only of values that genuinely occur. It should add that the range always sits inside the codomain and is often strictly smaller, which is exactly what the three unreached values on this slide are drawn to display.

questions.q: Using Domain Example 2, explain why the numerator of a fraction never restricts the domain, and state what would have changed if the denominator had been x² − 5 instead of x² + 5.
questions.concept: Only the denominator restricts the domain of a rational function
questions.why: A good answer says the numerator 3x + 1 is a polynomial, defined for every real x, so it can never fail; the only way a fraction becomes undefined is division by zero, which is a statement about the denominator alone. Her working confirms this: she writes down only x² + 5 ≠ 0 and never mentions 3x + 1 again. On the change: x² − 5 = 0 gives x² = 5 and hence x = √5 and x = −√5, both real, so those two values would have to be excluded and the domain would be every real number except ±√5 rather than (−∞, ∞). The point to draw out is that her method did not fail to find exclusions, it correctly found that there were none, and the same method finds them when they exist.

questions.q: Slide 22 asks for a table of f(x) = x + 2 at x = 0, 1, 2 and prints y = 2, 1, 0. Say what the printed table really belongs to, explain why the error is easy to overlook, and describe the habit that would have caught it.
questions.concept: Checking a table against the rule rather than trusting it
questions.why: A good answer identifies the printed values as the outputs of f(x) = 2 − x, not x + 2. It explains that the two functions agree at exactly one point, x = 0, where both give 2, so the first entry looks right and lends false confidence to the rest — and that both lines pass through (0, 2), so even a sketch would start out plausible. The habit: substitute each x into the printed rule independently rather than continuing a pattern, and sanity-check the direction — x + 2 has a positive coefficient on x, so y must increase as x increases, and a table that decreases contradicts the rule before any arithmetic is done. The correct table is 2, 3, 4.

questions.q: Slide 21 says a graph is made of the points (x, f(x)), and then says that for f(x) = x² the value increases exponentially. Explain what the first statement means and say what is wrong with the second.
questions.concept: Reading a graph as input-output pairs, and quadratic versus exponential growth
questions.why: A good answer explains the first claim as the definition of a graph: each point on the curve records one input and its output, the horizontal coordinate being the input and the vertical coordinate the value the rule assigns to it, so the curve is a picture of the whole function rather than a decoration. On the second: 'exponentially' is the wrong word. Exponential growth has the variable in the exponent, as in 2 to the power x; x² has the variable in the base and grows quadratically. The answer should note that the slide contradicts itself in the very next sentence by correctly calling the curve parabolic, and should say the right description out loud — x² increases quadratically, and its graph is a parabola opening upward.

questions.q: A negatively charged plastic rod is held close to, but not touching, an isolated neutral metal sphere resting on an insulating stand. What is the state of the sphere while the rod is held there?
options: The sphere acquires a net negative charge, because electrons leap across the narrow air gap onto it from the rod.
The sphere's net charge stays zero, but its near side is positive and its far side negative.
The sphere's near side becomes negative, since negative charge is drawn toward the rod.
Nothing changes inside the sphere at all, because the rod never touches it.
questions.concept: Polarisation of a neutral conductor by a nearby charge
questions.why: The rod's field separates charge inside the sphere - near side positive, far side negative - while the net charge stays zero because nothing crosses the air gap.

questions.q: During charging by induction the conductor is briefly connected to earth by a wire. What does that earth connection actually do?
options: It drains away all charge, leaving the conductor permanently neutral.
It supplies protons to the side of the conductor nearest the rod.
It shields the conductor from the rod's field so that charge can settle down.
It gives the repelled electrons somewhere to go, so an imbalance is left behind.
questions.concept: Function of the earth connection in charging by induction
questions.why: Earth is a charge reservoir into which the repelled electrons escape, so the sphere is left with a net imbalance once the ground connection is broken.

questions.q: A charged comb picks up small scraps of neutral paper, and does so whether the comb is charged positively or negatively. The best explanation is:
options: The comb polarises the paper; the nearer end is oppositely charged and so is pulled harder.
The paper carries a small leftover charge that happens to be opposite to the comb's.
The paper's protons drift toward the comb, producing a net pull toward it.
A neutral body has no charge that can be repelled, so any charged object can only ever attract it, at any distance.
questions.concept: Why a charged object attracts neutral matter of either sign
questions.why: The comb polarises the paper, and the induced opposite charge sits nearer the comb, so the attraction on it exceeds the repulsion on the farther like charge.

questions.q: Which of these net charges is impossible for an isolated object to carry?
questions.concept: Quantisation of charge as q = ne
questions.why: -2.4x10^-19 C is 1.5e, not a whole-number multiple of the elementary charge, so no isolated object can carry it.

questions.q: A plastic rod rubbed with wool ends up carrying −6 nC. What is left on the wool, and why?
options: −6 nC, because rubbing charges both surfaces negatively.
+6 nC, because the wool lost exactly the electrons the rod gained.
+6 nC, because protons moved from the wool onto the rod.
0, because only the rod becomes charged; the wool stays neutral.
questions.concept: Conservation of charge and electron-only transfer in friction
questions.why: The wool must hold +6 nC because it lost precisely the electrons the rod gained; protons never move between solids.

questions.q: The field at a point P near a fixed source charge is found by measuring the force on a small test charge q₀ and dividing by q₀. The test charge is then replaced by one of twice the size, still far too small to disturb the source. The value obtained for E at P:
options: doubles, because the force on the test charge doubles
halves, because the same force is now divided by a bigger charge
is unchanged, because the force and the divisor both double
quadruples, because the field depends on the square of the charge
questions.concept: Field as force per unit charge, independent of the test charge
questions.why: Doubling q0 doubles the measured force, and the ratio F/q0 is unchanged because E is fixed by the source alone.

questions.q: Bringing the charged rod closer to a neutral conductor increases the extent of the induction. The mechanism is that:
options: the conductor's net charge grows as the rod approaches
charge begins to leak across the shrinking air gap
the conductor gains extra free electrons that were unavailable further away
the rod's field at the conductor is stronger, so more free electrons are displaced
questions.concept: Why induction strengthens as the rod approaches
questions.why: Field strength rises as distance falls, so a stronger field displaces more of the conductor's free electrons before equilibrium is reached.

questions.q: You cannot charge a metal rod by rubbing it while holding it in your bare hand. Why not?
options: Any charge produced escapes through your body to earth.
Metals have no charge to separate, since their electrons are already free.
Friction cannot separate charge on a smooth metal surface.
The freed electrons immediately recombine with the metal's protons and cancel out.
questions.concept: Conductors and the human body as an earth path
questions.why: A metal rod held in the bare hand is continuously earthed through the body, so any charge separated by rubbing immediately leaks away.

questions.q: A charged rod attracts a neutral scrap of foil, yet two rods charged in the same way repel each other. Explain, in terms of what happens to the charges inside the foil, why attraction of a *neutral* object is not evidence that the foil is charged.
questions.concept: Attraction of a neutral object is polarisation, not evidence of net charge
questions.why: The rod's field separates charge inside the foil: the opposite charge is drawn to the near face and the like charge pushed to the far face. Because the Coulomb force falls off with distance, the attraction on the nearer opposite charge exceeds the repulsion on the farther like charge, so the net force is attractive. The foil's total charge is zero throughout, which is why two identically charged rods - both carrying real net charge of the same sign - repel instead.

questions.q: Charging by conduction leaves the conductor with the *same* sign as the charging rod, while charging by induction leaves it with the *opposite* sign. Explain why the difference in outcome follows from the difference in mechanism, and say what happens to the rod's own charge in each case.
questions.concept: Conduction shares charge; induction separates it and drains one sign away
questions.why: In conduction the rod touches the conductor, charge flows until both carry the same sign, and the rod loses some of its own charge in the process. In induction there is no contact: the rod's field pushes like charge to the far side, the earth connection lets that charge escape, and breaking the earth before removing the rod leaves the conductor with the opposite sign. The rod's own charge is unchanged in induction, because nothing ever crossed the gap.

questions.q: Two objects are rubbed together and both end up charged, one positive and one negative. Explain why this does not mean charge has been created, and state what observation would count as a violation of conservation of charge.
questions.concept: Conservation of charge in frictional charging
questions.why: Rubbing only transfers electrons from one surface to the other, so the negative charge gained by one is exactly the positive charge left on the other and the algebraic total is unchanged at zero. No charge was created - only separated. A violation would be a closed, isolated system whose net charge changed: both objects ending up negative, say, or an isolated body spontaneously acquiring charge with nothing else altering.

questions.q: The electric field is defined as force per unit charge rather than simply as the force felt at a point. Explain what would go wrong if physicists instead tabulated "the force at each point in space" around a charged object.
questions.concept: Force per unit charge makes the field a property of the source alone
questions.why: Tabulating 'the force at each point' would describe the source together with whatever test charge happened to be used, so a fresh table would be needed for every different test charge. Dividing by q0 removes the test charge from the description and leaves a quantity fixed by the source charges alone. That is what makes E predictive: multiply it by any charge later placed there to get the force on that charge.

It closes on the two kinds of program documentation, why documentation begins at problem analysis rather than after the program works, and on refactoring - what it must preserve, what it changes, and when a change is not a refactor at all.
