questions.q: The lesson insists that a programmer must first understand how a *human* would solve the problem before programming it. What is the reason?
options: A computer can only run a procedure that has already been proved correct by hand.
The computer supplies volume and speed, not method; it executes a procedure someone has worked out.
High-level languages cannot express a problem that has not been written out on paper first.
The CPU processes inputs in reverse order, so the human solution must be inverted before coding.
questions.concept: Why the programmer must understand the human solution first
questions.why: The computer supplies volume and speed but no method - it can only execute a procedure that has already been worked out, which is why the human solution must precede the program.

questions.q: What makes a problem a *computational* problem in the sense used in this course?
options: It can be answered YES or NO, which is the form a computer works in.
It is a real-world problem rather than an abstract one.
It is large enough that a human could not finish it by hand in reasonable time.
It has a step-by-step solution, and its inputs, limitations and output conditions are well defined.
questions.concept: The defining criterion of a computational problem
questions.why: A computational problem is one with a step-by-step solution whose inputs, limitations and output conditions are all well defined; being YES/NO, real-world, or large is not the criterion.

questions.q: A plan contains the step "keep adding the grades until you have enough of them". Which requirement on an algorithm's steps does this violate, and why does it matter?
options: Unambiguity — "enough" reads two ways, so no one definite statement can replace it.
Order — the step does not say whether the adding happens before or after the grades have been read into the program.
Completeness — the algorithm names no stop condition anywhere, so no further step could ever be reached from it.
None of them; the programmer supplies the missing detail during coding, which is exactly what the coding stage is for.
questions.concept: The 'unambiguous' requirement on an algorithm's steps
questions.why: 'Enough' has more than one reading, so no single definite programming statement can replace the step; the order is clear and a stop condition is implied, so it is unambiguity that fails.

questions.q: Pseudocode "looks like the actual program" but cannot be compiled or executed. What follows from that?
options: Pseudocode must be rewritten as a flowchart before it can be turned into a program.
Pseudocode is only useful for problems too small to need a compiler.
Nothing checks it for you, so an error in the pseudocode survives untouched into the source code.
Pseudocode is therefore not a representation of the algorithm, only an informal comment on it.
questions.concept: The consequence of pseudocode being non-executable
questions.why: Because no compiler or machine ever checks pseudocode, any error in it passes silently into the source code - which is why pseudocode must be reasoned over by hand.

questions.q: In the compilation and execution process described this week, what distinguishes an interpreter from a compiler?
options: The interpreter catches logical as well as syntax errors, whereas the compiler can only ever report syntax errors.
The interpreter goes straight to machine code; the compiler stops at assembly, which an assembler must still convert.
The interpreter works on low-level languages, while the compiler is the tool that works on high-level languages.
The interpreter produces the source code from the pseudocode, while the compiler produces the pseudocode itself.
questions.concept: Interpreter versus compiler in the translation chain
questions.why: The interpreter converts high-level language directly to machine code, whereas the compiler produces assembly language that still requires an assembler to reach machine code.

questions.q: Debugging and testing are named as separate activities. What separates them?
options: Debugging finds errors so they can be removed; testing verifies that the program does what was expected.
Debugging is done by the programmer, testing by the end user after the program is delivered.
Debugging deals with syntax errors, testing with logical and run time errors.
Debugging happens while coding, testing only after the program has been documented.
questions.concept: Debugging versus testing as distinct activities
questions.why: Debugging is the process that finds errors so they can be removed to avoid failure; testing is the process that verifies the program works as expected - a difference of purpose, not of who does it or when.

questions.q: Which change to a working program is a *refactor* in the sense the week defines?
options: Adding a check that rejects a negative grade, so wrong data no longer reaches the average.
Making the program run faster by no longer printing the grade alongside PASS or FAIL.
Correcting a division that used the wrong number of grades, so the average comes out right.
Replacing five repeated addition statements with one loop that produces the same output.
questions.concept: What refactoring must preserve
questions.why: Replacing five additions with one loop leaves the function of the solution untouched while improving structure and concision; the other options each change what the program does or fix a fault, neither of which is refactoring.

questions.q: The lesson advises that, when parts of a problem cannot be solved, you ignore the difficult parts and do the easier ones first. What is the actual cost of this tactic?
options: It produces code that cannot later be refactored, because refactoring requires a complete solution.
It reverses the four steps, since carrying out a partial plan comes before the plan is complete.
The easy parts may be built on assumptions the hard part later overturns, forcing that work to be redone.
None; the tactic is safe, because solving all the small problems automatically solves the main problem.
questions.concept: The cost of the 'ignore the difficult parts' tactic
questions.why: The easy parts get built on assumptions the postponed hard part may overturn, forcing rework - decomposition only guarantees the whole when the pieces are genuinely independent.

questions.q: Pseudocode cannot be compiled or executed, so writing it costs time and returns nothing runnable. Explain why it is still worth writing — what does it give you that going straight to source code does not?
questions.concept: What pseudocode buys you despite not being executable
questions.why: It forces the algorithm to be made explicit and complete in ordinary language before syntax gets in the way, so logical gaps are found while they are still cheap to fix. It is also language-independent, so the same plan can be coded in any language, and it doubles as documentation and as a way of communicating the design to people who do not read code. Going straight to source mixes two hard jobs at once: deciding what to do, and satisfying the compiler.

questions.q: Explain why a program can compile cleanly and run to completion without crashing and still be wrong. Name which of the three error types the week identifies is responsible, and say why the compiler is powerless against it.
questions.concept: Logic errors survive both compilation and execution
questions.why: A logic error is one where every statement is syntactically legal and nothing illegal happens at run time, so the program compiles and runs to completion - it simply computes the wrong thing. The compiler only checks that the code obeys the rules of the language; it has no access to the programmer's intention, so it cannot know that dividing by 5 was meant to be dividing by 4. Only testing against known expected answers exposes it.

questions.q: Explain why decomposition works — why solving every small subproblem should solve the main problem — and state one condition under which breaking a problem into pieces does *not* deliver a solution to the whole.
questions.concept: Decomposition and the independence condition
questions.why: Decomposition works because a large problem that is hard to hold in mind can be split into subproblems each small enough to solve directly, and the solved pieces then reassemble into the whole. It relies on the pieces being genuinely independent and on their interfaces being correctly specified. It fails when the subproblems are coupled - when the right solution to one depends on a choice made in another - so solving each in isolation yields pieces that do not fit together.

questions.q: Program documentation is said to begin at the problem analysis stage rather than once the program works. Explain why that timing matters, and why user documentation and programmer documentation cannot sensibly be merged into one document.
questions.concept: Documentation begins at problem analysis and serves two different audiences
questions.why: Starting at analysis captures the reasoning - what the inputs were taken to be, what was assumed, why a route was chosen - while it is still known; reconstructed afterwards, that reasoning is guesswork. The two kinds cannot sensibly be merged because they answer different questions for different readers: user documentation says how to operate the program and assumes no knowledge of its internals, while programmer documentation describes structure and logic so the program can be maintained and upgraded. One document attempting both serves neither reader.

checks.topic: Problems-only session on Week 1. Evaluate f(x) = 2x + 3 and f(x) = x² − 4 at negative inputs; find domains by setting the denominator ≠ 0, including the case her rendered examples never reach, where the exclusion is real; find ranges by making x the subject and by building up from |·| ≥ 0; find inverses by let–switch–isolate; form and expand both composites of f(x) = 5x − 4 and g(x) = x²; and work her TASK, the domain and range of √(x + 2) − 8, plus the corrected table from slide 22.

questions.q: For f(x) = 2x + 3, evaluate f(−4).
questions.concept: Substituting a negative input into a linear rule, multiply before adding
questions.why: 2(−4) + 3 = −8 + 3 = −5. Option 2 subtracts the constant instead of adding it, computing −8 − 3. Option 3 drops the minus sign on the input and evaluates f(4) = 11. Option 4 brackets the whole thing as 2(−4 + 3) = −2, which is the same order-of-operations slip that turns f(2) = 7 into 10 on her slide.

questions.q: For f(x) = x² − 4, evaluate f(−3).
questions.concept: Squaring a negative input before subtracting
questions.why: (−3)² = 9, so f(−3) = 9 − 4 = 5 — the same value as f(3), because squaring destroys the sign. Option 1 treats (−3)² as −9. Option 3 uses 2x in place of x², giving −6 − 4. Option 4 subtracts before squaring, (−3 − 4)² = 49, which is a different function altogether.

questions.q: Applying her denominator rule, what is the domain of f(x) = (2x − 1)/(x² − 9)?
options: All reals except 3
All reals except 3 and −3
All reals except 9
questions.concept: The denominator rule in the case where the exclusion is real
questions.why: Set x² − 9 ≠ 0, so x² ≠ 9, so x ≠ 3 and x ≠ −3 — both roots must go, because both make the denominator zero. Option 1 copies the answer of her Example 2 without redoing the algebra; there the equation had no real root, here it has two. Option 2 keeps only the positive root and forgets that (−3)² is also 9. Option 4 solves x² = 9 as though the square were not there. Note that she only ever displays the no-exclusion case on the surviving slides, so this is her rule applied where it actually bites.

questions.q: Using her method, find the range of f(x) = 5 − 4x.
options: All reals except 5/4
questions.concept: Range of a linear function by making x the subject
questions.why: Set y = 5 − 4x, then 4x = 5 − y and x = (5 − y)/4. That is a legal real number for every real y — nothing is divided by zero and no root is taken — so every output is attainable and the range is all of ℝ. Options 1 and 2 read the constant 5 as a ceiling or a floor, which happens with absolute values and squares but never with a straight line. Option 3 imports an exclusion from rational functions into a linear one. A line with non-zero gradient always has range (−∞, ∞).

questions.q: Following Range Example 3, find the range of f(x) = |x + 1| − 4.
questions.concept: Building a range upward from |·| ≥ 0 when nothing is multiplied by −1
questions.why: |x + 1| ≥ 0, and subtracting 4 from both sides gives |x + 1| − 4 ≥ −4, so y ≥ −4 and the range is [−4, ∞), with the bracket square because y = −4 is attained at x = −1. Option 2 reverses the inequality out of habit, but nothing here was multiplied by a negative — that reversal belongs to her Example 3, where the absolute value itself carried a minus sign. Option 3 keeps the direction but loses the sign of the constant. Option 4 forgets that an absolute value is bounded below and drags the range down to −∞.

questions.q: Using let–switch–isolate, find the inverse of f(x) = 4x + 9.
questions.concept: Sign handling when isolating y after the switch
questions.why: Let y = 4x + 9; switch to x = 4y + 9; isolate: 4y = x − 9, so y = (x − 9)/4. Check it: f(2) = 17 and (17 − 9)/4 = 2. Option 1 adds the 9 instead of subtracting when moving it across the equals sign — the commonest single error in this topic. Option 3 is the reciprocal 1/f(x), not the inverse. Option 4 reverses the operations in the right order but never divides by 4, so it undoes the +9 and not the ×4.

questions.q: With f(x) = 5x − 4 and g(x) = x², evaluate (g ∘ f)(2).
questions.concept: Evaluating a composite at a number, inner function first
questions.why: g ∘ f means f runs first: f(2) = 5(2) − 4 = 6, then g(6) = 6² = 36. It agrees with the expanded form 25x² − 40x + 16 at x = 2: 100 − 80 + 16 = 36. Option 1 is (f ∘ g)(2) = 5(4) − 4 = 16, the other order, and its difference from 36 is the whole point of her two examples. Option 2 comes from the wrong expansion 25x² + 16 at x = 2. Option 4 applies f and then forgets to square.

questions.q: In the style of her TASK slide, give the domain and range of h(x) = √(x − 5) + 3.
questions.concept: Square-root domain and the shift the constant applies to the range
questions.why: Under the root: x − 5 ≥ 0, so x ≥ 5 and D = [5, ∞). For the range: √(x − 5) ≥ 0, so √(x − 5) + 3 ≥ 3 and R = [3, ∞), both brackets square because x = 5 gives h(5) = 3 exactly. Option 1 gets the sign wrong when solving x − 5 ≥ 0. Option 2 finds the domain but forgets that the + 3 lifts every output by three. Option 3 forgets that a square root restricts the domain at all, which would only be true for an odd root.

questions.q: Work her TASK slide in full: find the domain and range of h(x) = √(x + 2) − 8, showing the inequality at every line, and justify the shape of each bracket in your answer.
questions.concept: The lecturer's own unanswered task, worked end to end
questions.why: A good answer treats the two parts by different methods, as she does. Domain: the quantity under a square root cannot be negative, so x + 2 ≥ 0 and x ≥ −2, giving D = [−2, ∞). Range: build upward from √(x + 2) ≥ 0, subtract 8 from both sides to get √(x + 2) − 8 ≥ 0 − 8, hence y ≥ −8 and R = [−8, ∞). On the brackets: both are square at the finite end because both endpoints are attained — x = −2 is a legal input and h(−2) = √0 − 8 = −8 is the actual smallest output — while ∞ always takes a round bracket because it is never reached. Credit an explicit note that subtracting 8 does not reverse the inequality, since nothing was multiplied by a negative.

questions.q: For f(x) = 5x − 4 and g(x) = x², compute f ∘ g and g ∘ f in full, expanding the square the long way as she does, and then show they are different by evaluating both at x = 3.
questions.concept: Both composites, expanded and then tested at a number
questions.why: A good answer writes f ∘ g = f[g(x)] = f[x²] = 5(x²) − 4 = 5x² − 4, with the brackets round x² so the 5 multiplies the whole square. Then g ∘ f = g[f(x)] = g[5x − 4] = (5x − 4)², expanded as (5x − 4)(5x − 4) = 25x² − 20x − 20x + 16 = 25x² − 40x + 16, showing both middle terms before collecting them — this is where the marks are, and the shortcut 25x² + 16 is the error the long expansion prevents. At x = 3: f ∘ g gives 5(9) − 4 = 41, while g ∘ f gives 25(9) − 120 + 16 = 121, which is also (15 − 4)² = 11² = 121. The two differ, so f ∘ g is not g ∘ f.

questions.q: Find the inverse of f(x) = 3x − 7, naming the three steps of her recipe as you use them, then verify your answer numerically.
questions.concept: The inverse recipe reproduced, with a numerical check
questions.why: A good answer labels the steps. Let: y = 3x − 7. Switch x with y: x = 3y − 7. Isolate the y variable: 3y = x + 7, then y = (x + 7)/3. So f⁻¹(x) = (x + 7)/3 — and it should write the argument, since her slide writes only f⁻¹ = (x + 7)/3. Verification: take any input, say x = 4, so f(4) = 3(4) − 7 = 5; feeding 5 back gives f⁻¹(5) = (5 + 7)/3 = 4, the original input, which is what an inverse is supposed to do. Credit an answer that also notes the reciprocal 1/(3x − 7) would have returned 1/5 here, not 4, and is therefore a different object.

questions.q: Slide 22 asks for f(x) = x + 2 at x = 0, 1, 2 and prints y = 2, 1, 0. Give the correct table, extend it to x = 3 and x = 4, list the points to plot, and state the gradient and y-intercept of the line they lie on.
questions.concept: Rebuilding the misprinted table and reading the line off it
questions.why: A good answer substitutes each value into the actual rule: x = 0 gives 2, x = 1 gives 3, x = 2 gives 4, x = 3 gives 5, x = 4 gives 6. The points are (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5) and (4, 6). Comparing consecutive points, y rises by 1 each time x rises by 1, so the gradient is 1, and the value at x = 0 is 2, so the y-intercept is 2 — both read straight off the rule y = x + 2. It should state plainly that the slide's printed values 2, 1, 0 are the outputs of 2 − x, a line of gradient −1 through the same intercept, and that the two agree only at x = 0.

checks.topic: This session takes the same week-1 material and works it as problems. It covers converting between a net charge and a number of transferred electrons using q = ne; tracking charge through transfers, including the averaging rule q' = (q1+q2)/2 for identical conducting spheres in contact and following a charge through two successive contacts; and computing Coulomb forces with attention to squaring the separation and converting centimetres to metres. It covers adding forces and fields as vectors, including the case of two equal and opposite charges whose contributions at the midpoint reinforce rather than cancel, and finding the point on a line where the resultant field vanishes. It covers computing the field of a point charge and the force it exerts on a charge placed in it, including the direction reversal for a negative charge. It also covers diagnosing a wrong route from the shape of a formula, and checking a result by units and by order of magnitude. Constants used throughout: k = 8.99x10^9 N.m^2.C^-2, e = 1.6x10^-19 C.

questions.q: An object carries a net charge of −4.8×10⁻¹⁷ C. How many excess electrons does it hold?
questions.concept: Converting a net charge to a number of electrons

questions.q: Point charges of +2.0 μC and −5.0 μC are held 4.0 cm apart in vacuum. The magnitude of the force between them is:
questions.concept: Coulomb's law with unit conversion and r squared

questions.q: Two identical metal spheres carry +9.0 nC and −3.0 nC. They are touched together and separated again. Each now carries:
questions.concept: Charge sharing between identical conductors, with signs kept
questions.why: q' = (+9.0 - 3.0)/2 = +3.0 nC on each sphere.

questions.q: A +2.0 μC charge sits at x = 0 and a +8.0 μC charge at x = 0.30 m. At what point between them is the resultant electric field zero?
options: 0.10 m from the 2.0 μC charge
0.15 m from the 2.0 μC charge
0.060 m from the 2.0 μC charge
0.20 m from the 2.0 μC charge
questions.concept: Locating the null point of two like charges
questions.why: Equal field magnitudes require (0.30 - x)/x = sqrt(8/2) = 2, giving x = 0.10 m, nearer the smaller charge.

questions.q: At a certain point the electric field is 2.0×10⁴ N·C⁻¹ pointing east. An electron is released there. The force on it is:
options: 3.2×10⁻¹⁵ N east
3.2×10⁻¹⁵ N west
8.0×10⁻²⁴ N west
1.3×10²³ N east
questions.concept: Force on a negative charge in a known field
questions.why: F = eE = (1.6x10^-19)(2.0x10^4) = 3.2x10^-15 N, directed opposite to E because the electron is negative.

questions.q: Asked for the field 4.0 cm from a +2.0 nC point charge, a student writes E = kQ/r = (8.99×10⁹)(2.0×10⁻⁹)/(0.040) = 450 N·C⁻¹. Which statement is correct?
options: The working is right; only the unit should be N·m·C⁻¹.
k is wrong here and should be ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹², giving 4.4×10⁻¹³ N·C⁻¹.
The separation must be squared, giving 1.1×10⁴ N·C⁻¹.
The charge must first be divided by e, giving 2.8×10²¹ N·C⁻¹.
questions.concept: Diagnosing a wrong route: 1/r versus 1/r^2
questions.why: The field law divides by r^2, so E = 17.98/(0.040)^2 = 1.1x10^4 N.C^-1, not the student's 450.

questions.q: Charges of +4.0 μC and −4.0 μC are fixed at points A and B, 20 cm apart. A +1.0 μC charge is placed exactly midway between them. The net force on it is:
options: zero, since the two charges are equal and opposite
3.6 N directed toward B
7.2 N directed toward A
7.2 N directed toward B
questions.concept: Vector superposition of two equal and opposite charges
questions.why: Both the attraction toward -4.0 uC and the repulsion from +4.0 uC point the same way, so the 3.6 N contributions add to 7.2 N toward B.

questions.q: Sphere X carries +8.0 nC. It is touched to identical neutral sphere Y and separated; Y is then touched to identical neutral sphere Z and separated. The final charge on Y is:
questions.concept: Conservation traced through two successive contacts
questions.why: X and Y each take +4.0 nC, then Y and Z halve that to +2.0 nC each, and 4.0 + 2.0 + 2.0 = 8.0 nC confirms the total is conserved.

questions.q: In a lab problem two small charged spheres about a metre apart carry charges of a few microcoulombs, and a student's answer for the force comes out as 4.0×10⁵ N. Explain why the size of that answer alone should tell you something has gone wrong, and describe how you would work backwards to locate the error.
questions.concept: Order-of-magnitude checking on a Coulomb's law result
questions.why: With charges of a few microcoulombs about a metre apart, F is roughly (9x10^9)(10^-6)(10^-6)/1, that is of order 10^-2 N - hundredths of a newton, not hundreds of kilonewtons. An answer of 4.0x10^5 N is about seven orders of magnitude too large, which points to a unit error rather than an arithmetic slip. Work backwards by checking the exponents one at a time: whether the microcoulombs were entered as 10^-6, whether the separation was squared, and whether centimetres were converted to metres.

questions.q: A student leaves the separation in centimetres in Coulomb's law. Explain why the answer is then wrong by a factor of 10⁴ rather than 10², and say whether the computed force comes out too large or too small.
questions.concept: Why a length-unit error is squared in Coulomb's law
questions.why: The separation enters the law as r^2, so any factor by which r is wrong is squared in the result. Leaving r in centimetres makes the number 100 times too large, and squaring that makes the denominator 10^4 times too large. The computed force therefore comes out 10^4 times too small.

questions.q: The field at a point can be found either as E = F/q₀ or as E = kQ/r². Show, by working through the units of each expression, that both must give N·C⁻¹, and explain why this is a useful check on a formula you half-remember.
questions.concept: Dimensional consistency of the two expressions for E
questions.why: F/q0 has units N/C directly. kQ/r^2 has units (N.m^2.C^-2)(C)/m^2 = N.m^2.C^-1/m^2 = N.C^-1, the same thing. This is a useful check because a half-remembered formula that has lost a power of r, or divided by the wrong quantity, will not reduce to N.C^-1 - the units fail before any arithmetic is done, so the error is caught early and for free.

questions.q: For two positive charges of different size, the point where the resultant field vanishes always lies nearer the *smaller* charge. Explain why this must be so without doing the algebra, and state what changes about the location of the null point if one of the charges is made negative instead.
questions.concept: Where the null point of two like charges must lie
questions.why: At the null point the two field magnitudes are equal. The larger charge produces the stronger field at any given distance, so to be matched by the smaller charge's field it must be viewed from further away - which places the null point nearer the smaller charge, and between the two for like charges. If one charge is made negative the two contributions no longer oppose each other between the charges; they reinforce there, so no null point exists between them and it moves outside the pair, on the side of the smaller charge.

checks.topic: This session is Week 1 applied - the method worked through on concrete problems. You trace the lecture's student-grade flowchart (five grades, average, pass mark 45, decision box "Is Grade > 44") on real numbers including the boundary case where the average lands exactly on 45, then alters the decision box to "Is Grade > 45" and works out precisely which candidates are misclassified as a result. He reads a faulty pseudocode that sums four grades but divides by five, identifies the fault and classifies it against the three error types, and reasons about which test inputs would and would not expose it. He runs step 1 of the four steps on the inventory management case study, separating genuine inputs, processes and outputs from outcomes and from the tools themselves, then decomposes that case study into subproblems and distinguishes real decomposition from mere phasing, delegation or file-splitting. He classifies stated scenarios into the four computational problem types, particularly the optimization-versus-search and decision-versus-search boundaries. Finally he diagnoses a failed attempt by another student and locates which of the four steps actually went wrong. Reading, tracing and applying rather than reciting.

questions.q: The lecture flowchart reads the five grades, computes Grade as their average, then asks "Is Grade > 44", printing PASS on the true branch and FAIL on the false branch. The grades entered are 40, 50, 45, 44, 46. What does it print?
options: FAIL, because the average works out at 44 and the pass mark is 45.
FAIL, because two of the five grades entered are themselves below the pass mark.
PASS, because three of the five grades are at or above the pass mark of 45.
PASS, because the average is 45 and 45 is greater than 44.
questions.concept: Tracing the grade flowchart on a boundary input
questions.why: 40 + 50 + 45 + 44 + 46 = 225, so Grade = 45; the box asks whether Grade > 44, which 45 satisfies, so the true branch prints PASS.

questions.q: A student decides the decision box is sloppy and rewrites it as "Is Grade > 45", saying the pass mark is 45 so the test should say 45. Who is now handled differently?
options: A student averaging exactly 45 is printed FAIL, although 45 is the pass mark.
Every student is printed FAIL, because a strict inequality can never hold on an average.
A student averaging exactly 44 is now printed PASS instead of FAIL.
Nobody; since grades are whole numbers, "> 44" and "> 45" select exactly the same students.
questions.concept: Off-by-one in the decision box
questions.why: '> 44' admits exactly 45 while '> 45' excludes it, so a student averaging precisely the pass mark of 45 is wrongly printed FAIL.

questions.q:
Someone hands you this pseudocode for the same task:

```
READ G1, G2, G3, G4, G5
Grade = (G1 + G2 + G3 + G4) / 5
IF Grade > 44 THEN PRINT "PASS" ELSE PRINT "FAIL"
```

What is wrong, and what kind of error is it?
options: A syntax error: the compiler will reject the second line because G5 is read but never used.
A run time error: the program will fail at the point where the unused fifth grade is reached.
A logic error: it runs to the end but averages wrongly, so only testing exposes it.
Nothing worth fixing: dropping one of five grades shifts the average by too little to change PASS or FAIL.
questions.concept: Classifying a fault that compiles and runs
questions.why: Summing four grades and dividing by five is syntactically valid and never crashes; it simply computes a wrong average, which is the definition of a logic error, and only testing against known answers reveals it.

questions.q: Working step 1 (understand the problem) on the inventory case study, which line correctly separates input, process and output?
options: Input: the reorder quantity. Process: the sales history. Output: the current stock level of the product.
Input: current stock level and sales history. Process: comparing stock against a reorder point. Output: the reorder quantity.
Input: lost sales and carrying costs. Process: the manager's judgement about demand. Output: an improved profit margin.
Input: the algorithm. Process: the flowchart drawn from it. Output: the pseudocode that the program is written from.
questions.concept: Applying step 1 to separate input, process and output
questions.why: Stock level and sales history are the data going in, comparing against a reorder point is the processing, and the reorder quantity is what comes out; the other options swap the roles, name an outcome rather than an output, or confuse the tools with the data.

questions.q: Which of these is a decomposition of the inventory problem in the sense step 2 means?
options: Restock all the fast-moving products first, and deal with the slow-moving ones in a separate later phase of the work.
Write the whole thing as one long program first, then split that finished program across several smaller source files.
Hand each branch manager the same inventory problem and let them solve it independently for the branch they run.
Record current stock; compute each product's sales rate; set a reorder point; order when stock drops below it.
questions.concept: What decomposition actually means
questions.why: Splitting the problem into smaller problems each small enough to solve - record stock, compute sales rate, set reorder point, raise order - whereas phasing, delegating and splitting files all leave the original problem intact.

questions.q: "Within a fixed storage budget, choose the stock mix that keeps total carrying cost as low as possible while never running out of the top ten sellers." Which computational problem type is this, and why?
options: Decision, because what is really being asked is whether the storage budget is sufficient.
Counting, because the number of product lines that fit inside the budget must be determined.
Optimization, because the best possible mix under stated limitations is what is accepted.
Search, because a stock mix having a particular stated property is what has to be found.
questions.concept: Optimization versus search
questions.why: A budget-constrained mix that keeps carrying cost as low as possible is one where the best possible solution is what is accepted, which is optimization; search would accept any mix with the stated property, not the best one.

questions.q: "At close of business, report whether any product at all has fallen below its reorder point." Which type is this?
options: Decision, because the solution is either YES or NO.
Search, because the products that have fallen below must be located and listed.
Counting, because the number below their reorder points has to be totalled up.
Optimization, because the best reorder point for each product is being determined.
questions.concept: Decision versus search
questions.why: The question asks only whether any product is below its reorder point, so the solution is YES or NO, which is a decision problem; naming or counting the products would be search or counting.

questions.q: Chidi opens his editor straight away and writes sixty lines from the case-study description. Only when it orders stock for products the store does not carry does he find that the sales file is keyed by supplier code, not product code. Which step failed?
options: Step 3, carrying out the solution plan — he compiled the program when he should have interpreted it.
Step 1, understanding the problem — he never established what the inputs actually were.
Step 4, evaluate and refactor — the working solution simply needs refactoring to accept supplier codes.
Step 2, creating the plan — his steps were ordered and unambiguous, but not complete.
questions.concept: Locating the failed step in someone else's attempt
questions.why: Chidi never established what the inputs actually were before writing code, so the failure is at step 1, understanding the problem - no amount of planning or refactoring rescues a misidentified input.

questions.q: Trace the lecture flowchart, box by box, on the grades 30, 60, 50, 40, 40. Name each box in the order it executes, give the value the process box produces, and say what is printed and why.
questions.concept: Tracing a flowchart box by box on given data
questions.why: Order of execution: Start; the input box reading G1..G5 as 30, 60, 50, 40, 40; the process box computing Grade = 220/5 = 44; the decision box 'Is Grade > 44?'; since 44 is not greater than 44 the false branch is taken; the output box prints FAIL; Stop. The process box produces 44, and FAIL is printed because the test is a strict inequality that 44 fails by exactly one mark.

questions.q: A classmate says the flowchart is wrong because FAIL is drawn on the left branch and PASS on the right, and "a flowchart always takes the left branch when the condition is true". Explain why the position of a branch on the page decides nothing, and say what actually determines which branch is taken.
questions.concept: Branch position on the page carries no meaning
questions.why: Which branch a flowchart takes is determined solely by the labels on the arrows leaving the decision box - the one marked true (or Yes) when the condition holds, the one marked false (or No) when it does not. Layout is a drafting convenience: the same chart may be drawn with the branches mirrored, rotated, or stacked one above the other, and it means exactly the same thing. There is no convention that true goes left, and a chart with unlabelled branches is ambiguous however it is drawn.

questions.q: Your grade program passes both of the tests you ran: 90, 90, 90, 90, 90 gives PASS and 10, 10, 10, 10, 10 gives FAIL. Explain why neither test would have caught the `(G1+G2+G3+G4)/5` fault from question 3, and give one set of five grades that would catch it.
questions.concept: Why unrepresentative test data hides a logic error
questions.why: The fault omits G5 while still dividing by 5, so the computed value falls short of the true average by exactly G5/5. With five 90s the true average is 90 and the faulty value 72 - both comfortably above 44, so PASS is printed either way. With five 10s the true average is 10 and the faulty value 8 - both well below 44, so FAIL is printed either way. Both tests sit far from the boundary, so an error of that size never changes the verdict. A set such as 40, 40, 40, 40, 90 catches it: the true average is 50 and should print PASS, but the faulty code computes 160/5 = 32 and prints FAIL.

questions.q: You replace the flowchart's five separate input boxes and its one long addition with a loop that reads a grade and adds it to a running total five times. Explain why this counts as refactoring under the week's definition, and state the one thing you must check before you are entitled to call it a refactor rather than a rewrite.
questions.concept: What makes a change a refactor rather than a rewrite
questions.why: It is refactoring because only the structure changes - five input boxes and one long addition become a single loop with a running total - while the function is untouched: the same five grades go in and the same average and the same PASS or FAIL come out. It improves concision and makes the number of grades easy to change. Before calling it a refactor you must check that the observable behaviour is identical on the same inputs, boundary cases included; if the loop reads a different number of grades, or the verdict shifts at the pass mark, it is a rewrite, not a refactor.

checks.topic: Culture's three components, the two society types, functionalism, colonialism's impact and nation-building.

questions.q: Which trio names the three fundamental components of culture?
options: Material, spiritual, political
Technological, economic, ideological
Technological, sociological, ideological
Sociological, ideological, historical
questions.concept: The three fundamental components of culture
questions.why: The course names technological (material culture), sociological (institutions and norms) and ideological (beliefs and values). The other three swap in economic, political or historical, none of which is one of the three.

questions.q: Communal and associational societies are distinguished on which three bases?
options: Division of labour, social interactions, traditions
Language, religion, territory
Division of labour, wealth, governance
Traditions, beliefs, material culture
questions.concept: The three bases separating communal from associational society
questions.why: The course fixes exactly three: division of labour, social interactions and traditions. The others borrow real course words (traditions, material culture, governance) but are not the stated three.

questions.q: Which view sees society as an organism where each part plays a crucial role?
options: Marx's communist society
National integration
Nation-building
Functionalism
questions.concept: Functionalism's organism metaphor
questions.why: Functionalism treats society as an organism whose every component serves the whole. Marx instead frames society around collective ownership of the means of production; the other two are processes, not theories of society.

questions.q: Colonialism is said to have altered which three domains of African societies?
options: Trade, warfare, language
Governance, culture, family structures
Religion, economy, technology
Governance, religion, education
questions.concept: The three domains colonialism altered
questions.why: The recap states governance, culture and family structures, with pre-colonial Yoruba communities as the worked example. The other options substitute domains the source never lists.

questions.q: Nation-building means mobilising resources for development and doing what else?
options: Removing ethnic diversity
Enforcing a single national language
Constructing a national identity
Collectivising the means of production
questions.concept: The two halves of the nation-building definition
questions.why: Both halves are needed: mobilising resources for socio-economic and political development plus constructing a national identity. Collectivising production is Marx; the other two are not part of the definition.

checks.topic: Internet vs Web, the request cycle, server types, and the tools you build with.

questions.q: Who introduced the World Wide Web, and in which year?
options: Sir Tim Berners-Lee, 1989
Sir Tim Berners-Lee, 1969
The ARPANET team, 1989
The ARPANET team, 1991
questions.concept: Origin of the World Wide Web
questions.why: Berners-Lee introduced the Web in 1989. ARPANET is the military network the Internet itself grew from, and 1969 belongs to that earlier story, not to the Web.

questions.q: If the Internet is the infrastructure, what is the World Wide Web?
options: The protocol browsers use to fetch pages
An application of hyperlinked pages running on it
The global network of interconnected devices
The system that maps addresses to servers
questions.concept: Internet versus World Wide Web
questions.why: The Web is one application built on the Internet: interconnected pages joined by hyperlinks. The protocol is HTTP, and the network of interconnected devices is the Internet itself.

questions.q: A user clicks a link. Which of these steps does NOT happen on the server?
options: Processing the request
Retrieving the requested resource
Rendering and displaying the content
Sending the HTTP response
questions.concept: Which side of the cycle renders the page
questions.why: Rendering is the browser's job: the server processes, retrieves and responds, and only then does the browser draw the page. Retrieving the resource and sending the response are both server steps in the four-step cycle.

questions.q: You type `https://miva.edu/notes.html` into the address bar. Which statement matches the week's URL and HTTP distinction?
options: The whole string is the protocol; the URL is only miva.edu
URL and HTTP are two names for the same addressing scheme
The URL is the request sent; HTTP is the reply that comes back
The whole string is the URL; https names the protocol that fetches it
questions.concept: URL is the address, HTTP is the protocol
questions.why: A URL is the address of a resource, and the protocol part states which rules fetch it. HTTP is not an address at all, so treating the two as the same thing collapses a distinction the week draws deliberately.

questions.q: A dashboard page is built fresh for each user out of database records. The week calls this:
options: Dynamic content generation
Load balancing
Request handling
Centralised data management
questions.concept: Dynamic content generation as a server function
questions.why: Dynamic content generation is a server building content on the fly from a request, usually by processing database data. Request handling is only accepting the request, and load balancing spreads traffic across machines.

questions.q: Every client reads the same orders from one database instead of its own copy. Which advantage of client-server is that?
options: Scalability
Separation of concerns
Centralised data management
Load balancing
questions.concept: The three advantages of client-server architecture
questions.why: Keeping one authoritative store that every client reads is centralised data management. Separation of concerns splits display from server logic, and load balancing is a server function, not one of the three advantages.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a server function rather than a browser function?
options: Bookmarking and history
Extensions and plugins
Rendering web pages
Data storage
questions.concept: Browser functions versus server functions
questions.why: Data storage sits in the server's five functions, next to request handling and dynamic content generation. Bookmarking, extensions and rendering are all on the browser's list, and only security appears on both.

questions.q: You want one program that edits, debugs and builds; a classmate wants a lightweight editor. Which pair fits the week's split?
options: Sublime Text for you, WebStorm for them
WebStorm for you, Sublime Text for them
Eclipse for you, Visual Studio for them
VS Code for you, Atom for them
questions.concept: IDE versus text editor
questions.why: WebStorm is an IDE, bundling debugging and build tooling; Sublime Text is a lightweight text editor. Eclipse and Visual Studio are both IDEs and VS Code and Atom are both editors, so neither of those pairs splits the roles.

questions.q: You need software that stores your HTML files and answers browser requests for them. Which named example fits?
options: MongoDB
Git
WebStorm
Nginx
questions.concept: Web server software among the week's examples
questions.why: Nginx is a web server: it stores and serves web content and handles incoming HTTP requests. MongoDB is a database server, Git is version control, and WebStorm is only the IDE you write the files in.

questions.q: You break `index.html` and want yesterday's working copy back. Which role of version control is that?
options: Branching and merging
Code collaboration
Version history
Code backup
questions.concept: The four roles of version control
questions.why: Version history keeps past versions so you can roll back or compare them. Code backup guards against losing the repository entirely, and branching is for developing features in parallel.

questions.q: Which trio names the three categories of web development tools?
options: Text editors and IDEs, developer tools, version control
Browsers, web servers and database servers
HTML, CSS and JavaScript
Editors, compilers and debuggers
questions.concept: The three categories of web development tools
questions.why: The week names text editors and IDEs, browser developer tools, and version control systems. The others are real course lists, but of servers, of core languages, or of tools the course never groups that way.

questions.q: Which of these tasks is back-end work?
options: Styling the checkout button with CSS
Querying the database for saved orders
Laying out the page with HTML
Showing a dropdown when a menu is clicked
questions.concept: Front-end versus back-end work
questions.why: Back-end work runs on the server and touches the database, which is exactly what querying saved orders does. The other three are things the user sees or clicks, so they are front-end.

checks.topic: The four language skills, their definitions, active versus passive listening, speaking components and writing styles.

questions.q: Listening is defined as the ability to do what with spoken language?
options: Hear and repeat it accurately
Understand, interpret and respond to it
Comprehend, interpret and analyse it
Articulate it coherently and effectively
questions.concept: The course wording of the definition of listening
questions.why: Listening is understanding, interpreting and responding to spoken language. Comprehending, interpreting and analysing is the definition of reading; articulating coherently is speaking.

questions.q: Background music playing without deep comprehension is the example of what?
options: Active listening
Hearing loss of context
Passive listening
Oral communication
questions.concept: Passive listening and its set example
questions.why: Passive listening is merely hearing without deep comprehension, and background music is its set example. Active listening is full engagement, with a lecture as the example.

questions.q: Which is NOT listed as a component of effective speaking?
options: Clear pronunciation
Voice control
Body language
Reading comprehension
questions.concept: The components of oral communication
questions.why: The components are clear pronunciation, appropriate tone, audience engagement, voice control, body language and delivery. Reading comprehension is a separate skill, not part of speaking.

questions.q: Which writing style explains a topic without arguing a side?
options: Persuasive
Narrative
Expository
Descriptive
questions.concept: Expository writing among the four styles
questions.why: Expository writing informs or explains neutrally. Persuasive takes a side, narrative tells a sequence of events, descriptive paints a static picture in detail.

questions.q: Extracting key findings from a research paper illustrates which skill?
options: Reading
Listening
Writing
Speaking
questions.concept: Classifying the set examples to the right language skill
questions.why: Reading is the written incoming skill, and the research paper is its set example. Summarising a TED Talk is listening, the job interview answer is speaking, the persuasive essay is writing.

checks.topic: The straight-line equation, linearising the pendulum, error types, percentage difference and the best-fit rule.

questions.q: In y = mx + c, what does c represent?
options: The gradient
The y-intercept
The x-intercept
The dependent variable
questions.concept: The terms of the straight-line equation
questions.why: c is the y-intercept, the value of y when x is zero. The gradient is m, and the x-intercept is minus c over m, found by setting y to zero.

questions.q: To linearise the simple pendulum, what is plotted against L?
options: T squared
T
ln T
log L
questions.concept: Linearising T = 2 pi root (L over g)
questions.why: Squaring gives T squared equal to (4 pi squared over g) times L, so T squared against L is a straight line through the origin. Logs are the tool for exponential decay and power laws, not for this one.

questions.q: Which error scatters both ways and shrinks when readings are averaged?
options: Systematic error
Zero error
Absolute error
Random error
questions.concept: Random versus systematic error
questions.why: Random error comes from unpredictable factors and averages out over repeats. Systematic error, such as an instrument zero error, has the same size and direction every time, so repeating never removes it.

questions.q: Which quantity keeps its sign, negative when the observed value is lower?
options: Absolute error
Relative error
Percentage difference
Percentage error
questions.concept: Percentage difference is signed; percentage error is a magnitude
questions.why: Percentage difference divides by a reference value and keeps its sign. Percentage error divides by the true value and is quoted as a magnitude; absolute and relative error are magnitudes too.

questions.q: The gradient triangle must be read from two points lying where?
options: On two raw plotted data points
On the drawn best-fit line
On the two axes
At the origin and one data point
questions.concept: Reading a gradient from the best-fit line
questions.why: Take two widely separated points that lie on the drawn best-fit line, so all readings contribute. Raw data points carry their own scatter, and the origin is only usable if the line actually passes through it.

recapCandidates.topic: Charging by induction versus charging by conduction: why contact leaves the same sign and no contact leaves the opposite one.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Both methods start with a charged rod near a conductor, so the two get filed as one procedure, and the earthing step is remembered as a place where charge is 'drained off' rather than as the step that selects which sign stays behind.
whyQuestions: Which particles actually move when any object is charged, and which never do?
In conduction, why do the rod and the sphere end up with the same sign?
In induction the rod never touches the sphere, so where does the sphere's charge come from?
Why must the earth connection be broken before the rod is taken away, and not after?
The rod loses charge in conduction but not in induction. Why does that difference follow from the mechanisms rather than being an extra fact to memorise?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It says that only electrons move, in both methods, and that the sign of an object is decided by whether it has gained or lost them.
It explains conduction as direct sharing on contact - charge flows until the two bodies are at the same potential, so both carry the same sign and the rod is left with less than it began with.
It explains induction as separation followed by selective removal: the rod's field pushes like charge to the far side, earthing lets exactly that charge escape, and breaking the earth first traps the imbalance, leaving the opposite sign while the rod's own charge is untouched because nothing crossed the gap.
recapCandidates.workedExample: A negatively charged rod is brought near an isolated metal sphere on an insulating stand. CONDUCTION: touch the rod to the sphere. Electrons flow from the rod onto the sphere until both are at the same potential. Remove the rod: the sphere is left negative, the same sign as the rod, and the rod is now less negative than it was. INDUCTION: hold the rod close without touching. The sphere polarises - near side positive, far side negative - but its net charge is still zero. Now earth the far side with a wire: the repelled electrons escape to earth. Break the earth connection while the rod is still held in place. Only now remove the rod. The sphere is left with a net POSITIVE charge, opposite to the rod, and the rod's own charge is exactly what it was at the start. If instead you removed the rod before breaking the earth, electrons would flow straight back from earth and the sphere would end up neutral - which is the single most common way this is got wrong.

recapCandidates.topic: Why a function must be one-to-one before it can be inverted, and why the domain - not the formula - is what decides.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Inversion is learned as the three-step algorithm (write y = f(x), swap x and y, solve for y), and the algorithm runs happily on functions that have no inverse, so it produces an answer that looks right and nothing in the procedure flags the problem.
whyQuestions: What does f-inverse actually do to a number, in one sentence, without mentioning the algorithm?
If f sends both 2 and -2 to 4, what would f-inverse(4) have to be?
Why does that make the reversed pairing fail to be a function, rather than merely being awkward?
The formula x^2 has no inverse on R but does on [0, inf). The rule never changed, so what did?
Given that, what is wrong with saying 'the inverse of x^2 is sqrt(x)' without further qualification?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It defines the inverse as the reverse pairing - f-inverse takes an output of f back to the input that produced it - so that f-inverse(f(x)) = x, and not as a rearrangement recipe.
It shows that a many-to-one f makes that reversal ill-defined: the shared output would need two images, which violates the very 'exactly one output' clause that makes something a function in the first place.
It concludes that a function is a rule together with a domain, so restricting the domain to make f one-to-one is what creates the inverse, and that the horizontal line test is the graphical form of exactly this check.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Take f(x) = x^2 on domain R. Run the algorithm anyway: y = x^2, swap to get x = y^2, solve to get y = +/-sqrt(x). The '+/-' is the algorithm telling you it has failed - for x = 4 it offers both 2 and -2, so the result is not a function and f has no inverse. Check it against the definition: f(2) = 4 and f(-2) = 4, so f-inverse(4) would have to be 2 and -2 at once. Graphically, the horizontal line y = 4 meets the parabola twice. Now restrict the domain to [0, inf). The pairs (-2, 4), (-3, 9) and so on are gone, every horizontal line now meets the curve at most once, and the same algorithm returns y = +sqrt(x) only, a genuine function. Note what swapped: dom f = [0, inf) and ran f = [0, inf), so dom f-inverse = ran f = [0, inf). Restricting instead to (-inf, 0] is equally valid and gives f-inverse(x) = -sqrt(x) - which shows the inverse depends on the domain chosen, not on the formula x^2.
